questions.question: Explain the main functions of the skeletal system and its importance to overall health.
questions.solution_html:
• Structure (7 marks)
  • Lymphatic system arises from tissue spaces as a meshwork of delicate vessels.
  • These vessels are called lymph capillaries.
  • Several lymph capillaries combine to form lymph vessels. All the lymph vessels
  • join to form two large ducts, left and right lymphatic duct which brings lymph
  • from right and left part of the body respectively. T
  • he left lymphatic duct is also known as thoracic duct. The right lymphatic duct
  • opens into the right subclavian vein and thoracic duct opens into the left
  • subclavian vein. Thus it reaches the circulatory system.
  • Lymphatic Capillaries
  • Lymphatic capillaries are vessels where interstitial fluid enters the lymphatic
  • system to become lymph fluid. Located in almost every tissue in the body, these
  • vessels are interlaced among the arterioles and venules of the circulatory system in
  • the soft connective tissues of the body.
  • Lymphatic capillaries are formed by a one cell-thick layer of endothelial cells and
  • represent the open end of the system, allowing interstitial fluid to flow into them
  • via overlapping cells. When interstitial pressure is low, the endothelial flaps close
  • to prevent backflow. As interstitial pressure increases, the spaces between the cells
  • open up, allowing the fluid to enter.
  • In the small intestine, lymphatic capillaries called lacteals are critical for the
  • transport of dietary lipids and lipid-soluble vitamins to the bloodstream. In the
  • small intestine, dietary triglycerides combine with other lipids and proteins, and
  • enter the lacteals to form a milky fluid called chyle. The chyle then travels through
  • the lymphatic system, eventually entering the liver and then the bloodstream.
  • Lymphatic Vessels
  • Lymphatic vessels are the network of capillaries and large network of tubes
  • located throughout the body that transport lymph away from tissues. Lymphatic
  • vessels collect and filter lymph (at the nodes) as it continues to move toward larger
  • vessels called collecting ducts. These vessels operate like our veins. They work
  • under very low pressure, have a series of valves in them to keep the fluid moving
  • in one direction.
  • Functions – ( 3 marks- ½ mark each for each point)
  • It maintains fluid levels in our body tissues by removing all fluids that leak out of
  • our blood vessels.
  • It carries nutrients and oxygen to different parts of body.
  • The lymphatic system is important for the optimal functioning of our general and
  • specific immune responses.
  • The lymph nodes monitor the lymph flowing into them and produce cells and
  • antibodies which protect our body from infection and disease.
  • The spleen and thymus are lymphatic organs that monitor the blood. They detect
  • and respond to pathogens and malignant cells.
  • The lymphatic system plays an important role in the absorption of fats from the
  • intestine.

questions.question: Discuss how autocrine signalling contributes to cancer progression. (10 x 2 = 20 marks)
questions.solution_html:
• a) Ribs and sternum
  • Autocrine Signaling
  • A cell releases molecules that bind to receptors on its own surface, producing a
  • response in the same cell.
  • Example: Cancer cells often use autocrine signaling to stimulate their own growth.
  • ● Types of Signaling Molecules
  • Hormones (e.g., insulin, TSH) – chemical messengers carried in blood.
  • Neurotransmitters (e.g., serotonin, acetylcholine) – transmit signals across synapses.
  • Growth factors (e.g., EGF) – regulate cell growth, division, and differentiation
  • Adrenalin, emotional stress, fear, pain etc increases WBC count.
  • Granulocytopenia: Decrease of granulocytes in blood
  • Synovial joint ( 5 marks)
  • The articulating surfaces of the bones are not directly connected instead they come into
  • contact with each other within a joint cavity that is filled with a lubricating fluid.
  • a) Pivot Joint
  • It consists of the round ended end of one bone fitting into a ring formed by the
  • other bone. This structure allows rotational movement as the rounded bone moves
  • around its own axis. An example is the joint of first and second vertebrae of the
  • neck that allows the head to move back and front.
  • b) Hinge Joint
  • In a hinge joint, the convex end of one bone articulates with the concave end of the
  • adjoining bone. This type of joint allows only for bending and straightening
  • motions along a single axis. Examples are elbow joint, the knee, ankle, and
  • interphalangeal joints between the phalanges of the fingers and toes.
  • c) Condyloid Joint
  • They are also known as ellipsoidal joint. The shallow depression at the end of one
  • bone articulates with a rounded structure from an adjacent bone or bones.
  • Condyloid joints are biaxial joints that allow for two planes of movement..
  • Examples are knuckle joint, wrist joint etc.
  • d) Saddle Joint
  • At a saddle joint, both of the articulating surfaces for the bones have a saddle
  • shape, which is concave in one direction and convex in the other. This allows the
  • two bones to fit together like a rider sitting on a saddle. The primary example is the
  • metacarpal bone at the base of the thumb.
  • e) Plane Joint
  • the articulating surfaces of the bones are flat or slightly curved and of
  • approximately the same size, which allows the bones to slide against each other.
  • The motion at this type of joint is usually small and tightly constrained by
  • surrounding ligaments. Plane joints are found between the carpal bones of the wrist
  • or tarsal bones of the foot.
  • f) Ball-and-Socket Joint
  • The joint with the greatest range of motion is the ball-and-socket joint. At these
  • joints, the rounded head of one bone (the ball) fits into the concave articulation (the
  • socket) of the adjacent bone. The hip joint and the shoulder joint are the only ball
  • and-socket joints of the body.

questions.question: Describe special types of passive transport
questions.solution_html:
• ● Passive transport moves substances across the cell membrane without energy
  • occurring along the concentration gradient (from higher to lower concentration) to
  • help maintain homeostasis (2 marks)
  • ● Bulk flow is the movement of large quantities of substances from high pressure to
  • low pressure, such as the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide across the
  • respiratory membrane. (1 marks)
  • ● Filtration is the movement of water and solutes from high hydrostatic pressure to
  • low hydrostatic pressure, seen in capillaries and kidney glomeruli. (1 marks)
  • ● Osmosis is the movement of water across a semipermeable membrane from lower
  • solute concentration to higher solute concentration. Types of osmosis include
  • endosmosis (water moving into the cell) and exosmosis (water moving out of
  • the cell). (1 marks)

questions.question: Describe skeletal muscles with diagram
questions.solution_html:
• Diagram (2 marks) , Structure (8 marks)
  • Skeletal muscle is situated in association with bones forming the skeletal system. The
  • skeletal muscles forms 40% to 50% of body mass and are voluntary and striated. They are
  • supplied with somatic nerve fibres.
  • Striated muscles are formed of large number of individual muscle cells known as muscle
  • fibres. They are multinucleated and cylindrical in shape. The fibres do not branch in
  • skeletal muscle.
  • Each muscle fibre is covered completely by a thin layer of plasma membrane called the
  • sarcolemma. It encloses a mass of protoplasm known as sarcoplasm. Sarcoplasm
  • contains several nuclei, numerous mitochondria and a network of smooth endoplasmic
  • reticulum called sarcoplasmic reticulum.
  • Each muscle fibre is formed of large number of longitudinal myofibrils. Each of them is
  • formed of delicate myofilaments which are arranged in repeating bundles or
  • compartments called sarcomeres. This arrangement gives the muscle fibre a banded or
  • striated appearance. Sarcomeres are structural unit of muscle fibres.
  • Each myofibril shows dark and light bands. The dark band has a high refractive index and
  • is called Anisotropic or A band. The light band is of low refractive index and is called
  • Isotropic or I band. In the middle of the light band is the Z line or Z membrane. A
  • sarcomere extends from one Z membrane to another Z membrane. The middle of the A
  • band is occupied by a region of lighter colour known as H zone.
  • Myofilaments are of two types – Thick and Thin. They are formed of proteins. Thick
  • filaments are formed of protein myosin and are also known as myosin filaments. Thin
  • filaments are formed by the protein actin and are also known actin filaments. In the
  • peripheral darker portion of A band both actin and myosin filaments are present. In the I
  • band only actin filaments are present where as in the H Zone only myosin filaments are
  • present.

questions.question: Explain structure and functions of lymphatic system
questions.solution_html:
• Structure (7 marks)
  • Lymphatic system arises from tissue spaces as a meshwork of delicate vessels.
  • These vessels are called lymph capillaries.
  • Several lymph capillaries combine to form lymph vessels. All the lymph vessels
  • join to form two large ducts, left and right lymphatic duct which brings lymph
  • from right and left part of the body respectively. T
  • he left lymphatic duct is also known as thoracic duct. The right lymphatic duct
  • opens into the right subclavian vein and thoracic duct opens into the left
  • subclavian vein. Thus it reaches the circulatory system.
  • Lymphatic Capillaries
  • Lymphatic capillaries are vessels where interstitial fluid enters the lymphatic
  • system to become lymph fluid. Located in almost every tissue in the body, these
  • vessels are interlaced among the arterioles and venules of the circulatory system in
  • the soft connective tissues of the body.
  • Lymphatic capillaries are formed by a one cell-thick layer of endothelial cells and
  • represent the open end of the system, allowing interstitial fluid to flow into them
  • via overlapping cells. When interstitial pressure is low, the endothelial flaps close
  • to prevent backflow. As interstitial pressure increases, the spaces between the cells
  • open up, allowing the fluid to enter.
  • In the small intestine, lymphatic capillaries called lacteals are critical for the
  • transport of dietary lipids and lipid-soluble vitamins to the bloodstream. In the
  • small intestine, dietary triglycerides combine with other lipids and proteins, and
  • enter the lacteals to form a milky fluid called chyle. The chyle then travels through
  • the lymphatic system, eventually entering the liver and then the bloodstream.
  • Lymphatic Vessels
  • Lymphatic vessels are the network of capillaries and large network of tubes
  • located throughout the body that transport lymph away from tissues. Lymphatic
  • vessels collect and filter lymph (at the nodes) as it continues to move toward larger
  • vessels called collecting ducts. These vessels operate like our veins. They work
  • under very low pressure, have a series of valves in them to keep the fluid moving
  • in one direction.
  • Functions – ( 3 marks- ½ mark each for each point)
  • It maintains fluid levels in our body tissues by removing all fluids that leak out of
  • our blood vessels.
  • It carries nutrients and oxygen to different parts of body.
  • The lymphatic system is important for the optimal functioning of our general and
  • specific immune responses.
  • The lymph nodes monitor the lymph flowing into them and produce cells and
  • antibodies which protect our body from infection and disease.
  • The spleen and thymus are lymphatic organs that monitor the blood. They detect
  • and respond to pathogens and malignant cells.
  • The lymphatic system plays an important role in the absorption of fats from the
  • intestine.
